question: A social network stored in an edge table must find friends of friends of friends. Why does a graph database suit this better than an RDBMS?

options.label: A
options.text: It stores pointers between connected nodes directly, so traversal does not rely on joins.
options.Explanation: This is index-free adjacency, which gives constant traversal time instead of repeated joins.

options.label: B
options.text: A graph cannot be represented in table form at all.
options.Explanation: A graph can be represented in a table, as the edge table with from, to and weight shows.

options.label: C
options.text: It stores the edge table by columns to compress it.
options.Explanation: Column storage belongs to column-oriented databases and does not address the cost of joins.

options.label: D
options.text: It keeps every node in a B-tree indexed by neighbour.
options.Explanation: Graph databases avoid relying on such an index for traversal, which is what index-free means.

hints: Think about what makes each extra hop costly in a relational table.

question: In a fraud graph, nodes are accounts and edges join accounts sharing a feature. Many unrelated accounts connect through a public computer. Which adjustment addresses this directly?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the time window on activities
options.Explanation: A tight time window reduces false positives, so removing it would make matters worse.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace the graph with a column-oriented table
options.Explanation: This changes the storage model without removing the false connections.

options.label: C
options.text: Give a shared IP address the highest edge weight
options.Explanation: A shared IP is treated as weak evidence with a low weight, unlike a shared credit card.

options.label: D
options.text: Filter out the supernode
options.Explanation: A public computer is exactly the example of a supernode to filter, because it links accounts that are unrelated.

hints: One node is linking far too many accounts for an innocent reason.

question: A graph has 9 nodes. Nodes 1–4 are connected to each other through paths, nodes 5–8 likewise, and node 9 has no edges. How many weakly connected components are there?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: This would need a path joining all the nodes, but the groups are separate.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: The two groups and the isolated node make three islands, and the number of components equals the number of islands.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: This overlooks node 9, which forms an island by itself.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: This counts every node separately, ignoring that the groups are connected.

hints: Count the islands, including any lone node.

question: A table has 6 rows and 3 columns. Each disk I/O reads 3 values. How many disk I/Os does summing the first column take in an RDBMS and in a column-oriented database?

options.label: A
options.text: 6 and 6
options.Explanation: The column store keeps the 6 values next to each other, so it needs fewer I/Os than one per value.

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 6
options.Explanation: These figures are reversed: it is the row layout that scatters the column's values.

options.label: C
options.text: 6 and 2
options.Explanation: In row order each 3-value read holds one value of the column, so 6 reads; the column store reads 6 adjacent values in 2.

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 2
options.Explanation: The row layout cannot fetch 6 scattered values in 2 reads of 3 values each.

hints: Lay out the values on disk for each design, then group them in threes.

question: A quant team stores hundreds of technical indicators per row but each study only computes the mean of a few of them. Which database type fits best, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: A column-oriented database, because it is read-optimized and reads only the needed columns
options.Explanation: Tasks touching a subset of many columns are its example of a good use, since other columns need not be read.

options.label: B
options.text: An RDBMS, because it is write-optimized
options.Explanation: Being write-optimized does not help a read-heavy workload on a few columns.

options.label: C
options.text: A graph database, because indicators are linked
options.Explanation: Nothing in this workload traverses relationships between nodes.

options.label: D
options.text: An in-memory key-value store, because it supports secondary indexes
options.Explanation: Redis indexes on the key only and has limited querying power.

hints: Compare how much data each storage layout must read for one attribute.

question: In a Bigtable holding (1, Name, 1 Jan 2020) → Diana and (1, Name, 1 Jan 2023) → Amy, why can both values coexist?

options.label: A
options.text: Row 1 is stored in two separate tables
options.Explanation: All data sits in one big table; the values differ only by timestamp.

options.label: B
options.text: Name is declared as a multi-valued column
options.Explanation: The structure is a map to a single string, so there is no multi-valued column.

options.label: C
options.text: The timestamp is part of the key, so each version has its own entry
options.Explanation: The map is keyed by row, column and time, which allows different versions to be retrieved.

options.label: D
options.text: A self-join merges the two names on read
options.Explanation: A self-join would rebuild a record from its entries; it does not explain how versions are stored.

hints: Look at what the map `(row, column, time) -> string` uses as its key.

question: Why does a wide-column database generally have higher read latency than an RDBMS, despite its fast writes?

options.label: A
options.text: It must lock every row before reading
options.Explanation: Its append-only mode is in fact praised for avoiding locking.

options.label: B
options.text: Null values have to be scanned
options.Explanation: Wide-column stores have no null overhead, since absent values are simply not stored.

options.label: C
options.text: It only stores data on magnetic disks
options.Explanation: The storage medium is not the reason given; the cost lies in the data structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Finding the latest data in LSM trees takes more effort
options.Explanation: Versions are spread across immutable sorted records, so locating the newest one costs extra work.

hints: Consider what append-only writes leave behind for a reader to sort out.

question: In an LSM tree, what happens to outdated or deleted records?

options.label: A
options.text: They are overwritten in place at update time
options.Explanation: An append-only design inserts a new version rather than updating in place.

options.label: B
options.text: They are cleaned up as data is merged and compacted in the background
options.Explanation: The continuous background merge and compaction removes deleted or outdated records.

options.label: C
options.text: They stay on disk permanently, because records are immutable
options.Explanation: Records are immutable once flushed, but compaction still replaces them with cleaned ones.

options.label: D
options.text: They are removed from the memory buffer before any flush
options.Explanation: Older versions may already be on disk, so the buffer cannot be the only place cleaned.

hints: Think about the step that continues after records have been flushed to disk.

question: Enrollment records in Cassandra store only student ID and module code. A user asks for the names of the modules taken by Amy. What difficulty does this expose?

options.label: A
options.text: CQL has no JOIN operator, so combining the data is poorly supported
options.Explanation: Finding the names requires joins, and poor support for those is a stated problem of wide-column databases.

options.label: B
options.text: Cassandra cannot store text values
options.Explanation: Values in the data model are strings, so text is not the issue.

options.label: C
options.text: Writes would block until the query completes
options.Explanation: Fast, append-only writes are an advantage and are not the problem here.

options.label: D
options.text: Horizontal scaling forbids any lookup by student ID
options.Explanation: Scaling out does not prevent key lookups; the missing piece is combining records.

hints: Count how many separate kinds of record the answer draws on.

question: Redis stores sessions under keys such as `session:auth:98342`. Why is finding all sessions with `status` equal to `authenticated` a poor fit?

options.label: A
options.text: RAM is too slow for scanning values
options.Explanation: RAM is the fastest of the benchmarked media, so speed of the medium is not the issue.

options.label: B
options.text: JSON values cannot be stored in Redis
options.Explanation: The sample data shows such a structured value stored against a key.

options.label: C
options.text: Redis has an index on the key only, with no secondary index on other fields
options.Explanation: A query on `status` is not on the key, and this limited querying power is a stated trade-off.

options.label: D
options.text: Hashed sharding deletes non-key fields
options.Explanation: Sharding spreads data across nodes and does not remove any fields.

hints: Which field does the Redis index cover?

question: A Redis server restarts after a power failure and rebuilds its data by re-executing every logged write. Which persistence option is this?

options.label: A
options.text: Snapshot
options.Explanation: A snapshot restores a point-in-time copy of the dataset rather than replaying each operation.

options.label: B
options.text: NVRAM
options.Explanation: NVRAM is a type of memory, and the current Redis does not use it as primary memory.

options.label: C
options.text: Hashed sharding
options.Explanation: Sharding distributes data across nodes and is not a persistence method.

options.label: D
options.text: AOF (Append Only File)
options.Explanation: AOF logs every write operation received, and replays them at startup to reconstruct the dataset.

hints: The mechanism records operations rather than the state of the data.

question: The text `The Apple ran` passes through the character filter, tokenizer, normalization, stopword filter and stemming filter. What are the final terms?

options.label: A
options.text: [the, apple, ran]
options.Explanation: This skips the stopword and stemming filters, which remove the and map ran to its root.

options.label: B
options.text: [Apple, ran]
options.Explanation: This skips normalization and stemming, which would change the case and the verb form.

options.label: C
options.text: [apple, run]
options.Explanation: Tags are removed, the text is split and lower-cased, the stopword is removed, and ran is stemmed to run.

options.label: D
options.text: [the, apple, ran]
options.Explanation: The character filter removes HTML tags before tokenizing.

hints: Apply the stages in order and write the tokens after each one.

question: A term appears in all 3 documents of a corpus. What are its textbook IDF and its scikit-learn IDF?

options.label: A
options.text: Textbook 1, scikit-learn 0
options.Explanation: These are swapped: the added $+1$ belongs to the scikit-learn version.

options.label: B
options.text: Both 0
options.Explanation: Scikit-learn adds 1 after the logarithm, so its value cannot be 0 here.

options.label: C
options.text: Both 1
options.Explanation: The textbook value is $\log_{10}(3/3)=0$, not 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Textbook 0, scikit-learn 1

hints: Substitute $N=3$ and $\text{df}(t)=3$ into each formula.

question: A document's TF-IDF vector before normalization is $(3, 4)$. What is it after L2 normalization?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: The L2 norm is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$, and each entry is divided by it.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: This divides by the sum of the entries instead of the L2 norm.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: This divides by the largest entry instead of the L2 norm.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: This squares the entries but never divides by the norm.

hints: Compute the square root of the sum of squares first.

question: A term appears 50 times in one document and 10 times in another. Which description matches how BM25 improves on TF-IDF here?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the weight exactly 5 times larger, in proportion to the count
options.Explanation: Linear growth is the TF-IDF problem that BM25 is designed to fix.

options.label: B
options.text: It caps the rate at which term frequency increases the score
options.Explanation: This is term frequency saturation, reflecting that relevance does not increase linearly.

options.label: C
options.text: It ignores term frequency and uses only document length
options.Explanation: BM25 still uses term frequency, through a modified function.

options.label: D
options.text: It removes all tuneable parameters
options.Explanation: BM25 adds tuneable parameters, whereas lack of tuning is a problem of TF-IDF.

hints: Relevance does not grow in proportion to the count.

question: Vectors $x=(3,4)$ and $y=(4,3)$ are compared. What is their cosine distance?

options.label: A
options.Explanation: This is the cosine similarity; the distance is 1 minus this value.

options.label: B
options.Explanation: Similarity is $\frac{12+12}{5\times5}=0.96$, so the distance is $1-0.96$.

options.label: C
options.Explanation: This is only the dot product, without dividing by the magnitudes.

options.label: D
options.Explanation: This is only the product of the magnitudes.

hints: Find the cosine similarity first.

question: A search application needs exact k nearest neighbour results and accepts slower queries. Which method meets the requirement?

options.label: A
options.text: IVF, because it searches only candidate clusters
options.Explanation: Narrowing to candidate clusters gives approximate results only.

options.label: B
options.text: HNSW, because it refines results at the ground layer
options.Explanation: Despite the refinement, HNSW also gives approximate results only.

options.label: C
options.text: Keyword search, because it matches exact words
options.Explanation: Matching keywords does not measure vector closeness, and is no kNN search.

options.label: D
options.text: Brute-force calculation, at $O(n)$
options.Explanation: Comparing the query with every vector is the only listed method not described as approximate.

hints: Two of the methods carry the warning that they are approximate.

question: A team must choose a vector index. Their data changes often and fast search matters more than RAM. Which choice and reason fit?

options.label: A
options.text: IVF, because it uses less memory
options.Explanation: Saving RAM is IVF's advantage, but it is the lesser priority for this team.

options.label: B
options.text: IVF, because it searches in $O(\lg n)$
options.Explanation: Average IVF search is $O(\sqrt{n})$; the logarithmic figure belongs to HNSW.

options.label: C
options.text: HNSW, because it is faster and needs no re-training
options.Explanation: It searches in $O(\lg n)$ on average and does not rely on K-means clustering.

options.label: D
options.text: HNSW, because it gives exact results
options.Explanation: HNSW gives approximate results only.

hints: Match each stated priority to an advantage in the comparison.

question: During an HNSW search, why does the process move down through the layers?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower layers are denser, so there are more potential closer neighbours to discover
options.Explanation: Higher layers are sparser subsets, and only the ground layer contains every vector.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower layers hold the K-means cluster centres
options.Explanation: K-means clustering belongs to IVF, not HNSW.

options.label: C
options.text: Upper layers contain only outdated vectors
options.Explanation: Upper layers are sparser subsets of the data, not stale copies.

options.label: D
options.text: Each lower layer holds a different dataset
options.Explanation: Each higher layer is a subset of the lower layer, so the data is shared.

hints: Compare the number of points in each layer.

question: Why might a semantic search return a chunk about "automobile repairs" for the query "fixing my car" when a keyword search would not?

options.label: A
options.text: The chunk is matched by edit distance
options.Explanation: Edit distance suits typos, and "automobile" is not a misspelling of "car".

options.label: B
options.text: Semantically similar texts have close embedding vectors
options.Explanation: kNN on the query vector finds close chunks even without a shared keyword.

options.label: C
options.text: The inverted index maps every term to all documents
options.Explanation: An inverted index maps a word only to documents containing that word.

options.label: D
options.text: BM25 ranks long documents highest
options.Explanation: BM25 is a keyword relevance score, and it does not create matches on unshared words.

hints: Consider what closeness between vectors represents.
